questions.text: What does the go statement do?
options: Starts a function call as a new goroutine
Blocks the current goroutine until the call finishes

questions.text: Where are the arguments of go f(x) evaluated?
options: In the new goroutine, before f’s body
In the current goroutine, before the new one starts

questions.text: What happens to other goroutines when main returns?
options: The process exits and they are stopped
They are turned into OS threads

questions.text: Can you assign the result of a function started with go?
options: Yes, if f returns one int
No. go f() is a statement and yields no values

questions.text: Does recover in main catch a panic in another goroutine?
options: No. recover only works in the panicking goroutine
Yes, if recover is in main’s defer

questions.text: What must follow go syntactically?
Are goroutines 1:1 with OS threads?
options: Yes, each goroutine is its own thread
No. Many goroutines are multiplexed onto fewer threads

questions.text: Is a goroutine guaranteed to run if main returns right away?
options: Yes, the runtime waits for its first line
Yes, if the function is short
Yes, go is always synchronous for one step
No. Leaving main ends the process with no such promise

questions.text: go f() waits for f to finish before the next line runs.
The go statement cannot return values to the caller.
A panic in a goroutine without recover crashes the whole program.
recover in the panicking goroutine can stop the panic.
Every goroutine always runs in parallel on its own core.
Each go creates a new OS thread.
Arguments of a go call are evaluated before the new goroutine starts.
Unfinished goroutines keep the process alive after main returns.
What does go f() start?
questions.answer: A new goroutine that runs the call f().

questions.text: Where is x evaluated in go f(x)?
questions.answer: In the goroutine that executes go, before the new one starts.

questions.text: What happens to the program when main returns?
questions.answer: The process exits; other goroutines are stopped.

questions.text: Does go f() yield values you can assign?
questions.answer: No. It is a statement, not an expression.

questions.text: Will recover in main catch another goroutine’s panic?
questions.answer: No. Only recover in that same goroutine.

questions.text: What must come after the go keyword?
Is a goroutine an OS thread?
questions.answer: No. Many goroutines share a smaller set of OS threads.

questions.text: Must a goroutine run if main has already returned?
questions.answer: No, there is no such guarantee.
